mcqs.question: A URL shortener sees a 100:1 read:write ratio. What does that ratio tell you to optimize first?
options: The redirect (read) path, since it dominates total traffic by two orders of magnitude
The write path, since writes are the rarer and therefore more valuable operation
Neither — both paths see identical traffic once caching is added
The Key Generation Service, since it is the only stateful component
mcqs.explanation: A 100:1 ratio means reads vastly outnumber writes, so the redirect path is what an architecture must handle cheaply and reliably — that's why caching is the first mechanism introduced. Writes still matter but are far lower volume; the KGS is important but isn't where the traffic volume actually is.

mcqs.question: Why do most production URL shorteners use a counter fed by a pre-shuffled range rather than a plain hash of the URL?
options: Hashing is computationally too slow to run on every write
A counter guarantees no collisions, avoiding retry logic, while shuffling avoids the sequential-guessing problem of a raw counter
Hashes cannot be represented in base62
Counters require no database at all
mcqs.explanation: A plain counter is collision-free but predictable (code N+1 always follows N); a plain hash avoids predictability but needs collision retries. Pre-shuffling a counter's output range gets both: guaranteed uniqueness with no obvious sequence. Hashing isn't meaningfully slow, and base62 encoding works fine on hash output too.

mcqs.question: Why does a cache holding only a small percentage of all short codes still absorb the vast majority of redirect traffic?
options: Because the cache automatically stores every code that has ever been created
Because link click volume follows a power law — a small fraction of links receive most of the clicks
Because 301 redirects make caching unnecessary
Because the database is too slow to serve any request directly
mcqs.explanation: Real click distributions are heavily skewed: a small set of popular links account for most traffic, so caching just that hot set covers most requests. The cache doesn't store everything (that would defeat the purpose), and this has nothing to do with which HTTP redirect status is used or the database's raw speed.

mcqs.question: Your product needs per-click analytics on every shortened link. Which redirect status code should you use, and why?
options: 301, because permanent redirects are always the correct default for shorteners
Either works identically for analytics purposes
Neither — analytics requires a 200 response with a JavaScript redirect
302, because 301 responses get cached by browsers/CDNs and you'd stop seeing repeat clicks
mcqs.explanation: A 301 gets cached client-side, so repeat visits never reach your server again — you lose visibility into those clicks. A 302 is never cached, so every click is observed, at the cost of more server load (which the caching layer already absorbs). A JS-based redirect isn't needed and adds latency.

mcqs.question: Why should click-analytics recording happen asynchronously rather than as part of handling the redirect request?
options: Synchronous writes would block or slow down the redirect response the user is actively waiting on
Analytics events are optional and can be skipped entirely
Message queues are cheaper than databases
Asynchronous processing is required by HTTP for all 30x responses
mcqs.explanation: The user is waiting for the redirect itself, not for an analytics write to commit — coupling the two adds latency and a new failure mode to the one truly latency-critical path. Async publishing (to a queue, consumed separately) decouples them. Analytics matters for the product; it's just not on the hot path.

mcqs.question: What's the main risk of using a base62-encoded auto-increment database ID directly as a short code?
options: It makes the redirect path slower
It's incompatible with custom aliases
It exposes total link volume and lets anyone enumerate the platform's links by walking adjacent codes
It requires storing the mapping table unsharded
mcqs.explanation: A sequential ID, however encoded, reveals creation order and total volume, and lets an attacker enumerate every link by incrementing the code — an information-disclosure and scraping risk. It has no effect on redirect latency, custom aliases, or sharding decisions.
